post.title: Ask HN: Is it impossible to disable Siri on macOS 27?

content.text:
I disabled Siri in the Settings app, and then further disabled Siri and its extensions in Settings > Screen Time.

Next, I disabled all Siri-related and Apple Intelligence-related services as per https://github.com/OleksandrKrupko/mac-os-debloat

But after restarting, I could still see a "Siri" process running in Activity Monitor. Upon further inspection, I found that it is the "Siri AI.app".

These "features", together with Apple's Personal Context sound very similar to Microsoft's Recall.

Does anyone have the same experience? Is it really impossible to fully turn off Siri, Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and all related services and features on macOS 27?

Just as a note, from what I see the problem is not only the privacy implications but also that the local AI comes with a baggage amounting to 10% of the space on the base mac models. Which is already severely limited. reply

I have not found the local/remote hand off to be very reliable either, so tasks that used to be almost instantaneous for Siri are now spinning to the point where I assume they failed. A simple 2 minute timer took almost 30 seconds to set the other day. reply
You're brave. I'm still on Sequoia. reply

I've been daily-driving a mac for 10 years now and I've only ever triggered Siri by accident.  I do use it pretty regularly on the phone, mostly to set timers, get directions, and call contacts, but I've been well trained over these years to not expect it to be capable of more than that. reply

I remember it being pretty useful on phone. Now, it can't even "like" a song when I'm driving and I want it to add a song to my Spotify favourites list. It could do a few months ago, now it refuses with "sorry there was a problem with the app". I've had to resort to asking it to take a screenshot so I can go find the song later. Three quarters of the time it never saves the screenshot though, despite seeing the screen flash out of the corner of my eye. reply
> now it refuses with "sorry there was a problem with the app". > I want it to add a song to my Spotify favourites list There's your problem reply
Your training is now out of date. reply

One workaround that I know would work would be an enterprise profile. I know this because I’m one of the people tasked with blocking AI stuff at my org. How you’d implement this without a subscription to management (MDM) software I leave to you to research. I know it’s possible without proprietary tools because I’ve read about people using profiles to block software updates on their personal computers, but I don’t recall how that’s done. reply
You can just use Apple Configurator to make a .mobileconfig file and apply that, no MDM required. reply

There’s the old trick of setting your computer language to be different from the Siri language. I get the following error message when I open Siri in Settings: > Apple Intelligence requires that Mac and Siri are set to the same language. Currently your Mac is set to English (United States) and Siri is set to English (Canada). I think at one point they may have removed this limitation but then they reintroduced it in macOS 27.0. reply

Yes, I did something similar: prior to disabling Siri, I set Siri's language to French and kept the system language set to English (UK), but the Siri AI.app ("Siri" process in Activity Monitor) just keeps running despite Siri being indicated as disabled in Settings. If you are on macOS 27, could you please open Activity Monitor, search (filter) for "siri" and see if a process called "Siri" is still running? reply

You are right. The UI shows Siri disabled and offers to turn it on, but the process is still running. That process seems to change its name based on whether the UI thinks Siri is enabled; it can be called either just "Siri" or "Siri AI" but it’s the same executable. reply
In Screen Time -> Content and Privacy, there's a setting to switch Siri to 'Siri Classic' which strips out the Apple Intelligence-backed behavior specifically. reply
Instead of "Siri Classic", I selected the "Don’t Allow Siri" option, but it didn't help. The "Siri" (Siri AI.app) process keeps running regardless. reply
Sounds like Apple hired some of the Microsoft project managers. reply
The process that shows the Spotlight UI is now the one called "Siri", previously it was called "Spotlight". reply

Thanks, that's an interesting observation! When I double-clicked on the "Siri" process in Activity Monitor, I saw that it's an app called "Siri AI". If the "Siri AI" app has replaced Spotlight, then I wonder if Apple keeps building "personal context" despite Siri and Apple Intelligence being disabled. It for sure doesn't sound well to disable Siri and still see a "Siri" process. reply
Couldn’t it be due to spotlight being entirely replaced by this new Siri AI? Not sure how things work under the hood now. reply
I've love to disable Apple Intelligence just to get the space back. It's murdering my Mac Mini. reply
Resistance is futile. reply
you will be assimilated reply
See https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49787535 reply
I didn't check it yet but I hope being in EU macOS 27 upgrade is basically small UI tweaks and thats it :D Still holding off for now reply

Try disabling any of the launchd tasks related to it, odds are theres a service that starts at boot/login regardless of any user-facing setting that do nothing if they're all turned off (just like iCloud related daemons). Odds are you'll probably run into something that requires you to disable SIP, like I did when I got tired of mediaanalysisd eating up CPU cycles on a 2018 Mac mini. reply

Thanks, I believe this is what the debloat script mentioned in my post does. I manually executed the `launchctl bootout` and `launchctl disable` commands on all Siri and AI-related services in the https://github.com/OleksandrKrupko/mac-os-debloat/blob/main/... script, but the "Siri" process ("Siri AI.app") still keeps running even after restarting. The Siri AI.app is read-only, so I could not even remove it. But perhaps it would be possible to boot into Recovery, mount the system partition as rw and delete the Siri AI.app from the filesystem? P.S. I did also disable mediaanalysisd and photoanalysisd, and those are NOT running. However, the Siri AI.app does keep running... reply
if you dont want a car with the hood welded shut.....Dont buy a car with the hood welded shut. plenty of better operating systems out their reply
Plenty of other operating systems out there ? Yeah. Better? Depends. Hardware as a package? Absolutely not and it’s by such a wide margin there’s no competition whatsoever. reply
Silly argument. It’s more like buying a BWM and being happy with everything expect a stupid decision like placement of the handbrake. Of course you can complain about it. reply
I don’t particularly care for MacOS but Apple’s hardware is generally best in class, particularly for battery life, touchpad, and other laptop specifics. reply

I still have to find anybody using Siri on his Mac Please tell me what the use case is. Somebody somewhere must find it useful otherwise it would not be so prominent. This a genuine question btw not trying to be sarcastic or dismissive reply
The 27 release still has so many bugs. It's depressing to see certain bugs persist in each new beta. You know they'll be in release. I gave up reporting anything years ago. reply
Sequoia will be taken from my cold dead hands. reply

Same here. Unfortunately, if you use Xcode to develop for iOS, then Apple basically forces you to install macOS 27 to be able to develop for the new iPhones. The iPhone 18 Pro requires Xcode 27, and Xcode 27 won't run on Sequoia. If anyone knows how to make the iPhone 18 Pro work with Xcode 26 on Sequoia, and in turn with iOS 27, I (and I'm sure many other people) would be very happy to hear how! reply
This is how Apple have forced Mac upgrades for the last 20 years, there is no way round it other than to comply and buy yourself a new Mac. reply

I started de-googling a long time ago, part of it was an iPhone (12 mini), 5 years later I really felt like de-Appling as well. The Appstore is a cesspool, privacy concerns are about the same as Google now (or perhaps always were?). I went with GrapheneOS. Very good experience, but not without Google Play (store and services). It's all sandboxed, so presumably I'm only leaking consciously chosen data. It's really aimed at security, not so much de-googling. Something like Murena's /e/OS is much more aimed at de-Googling, but as GrapheneOS devs will usually be quick to point out here, they are "quite poor" with their security. A de-Googled functional appstore on a FairPhone (+ with all the GrapheneOS required security bells and wistles) would be ideal for me. But it's still either optimal security focussed OR de-Googling/de-big-teching focused. Yes there is f-droid, but there are too many apps that require the Google services (like banking). Atm 1 app does not work, one of my banking apps required the highest tier of Google control. I will happily install on devices that have been years without security updates though :s Overall the GrapheneOS experience (base launcher etc) is very clean, fast, minimal, ad free. reply

People have a low tolerance for dupe posts, especially if they're perceived as excessive self-promotion. Also, your work might be seen as vibecoded and therefore "ai slop". I dont know if it is, but all it takes is a perception. Finally, your work might be seen as a commercial threat by some people here - causing them to flag it. > how i can share my work with HN community Write a technical article about some aspect of what you've done. tl;dr: go to protondb.com, search for Diablo 4, and then filter the list of results by "Distro" for Ubuntu (and Mint), and try the options that people say worked for them ProtonDB is a site that aggregates reports from users of Proton, the compatibility layer to let Windows games run on Linux. The usual solutions are switching the Proton version you use and/or commands you add to the custom commands in the configuration for that particular game in the Steam menu. There are also successful reports from people on Linux Mint, which is based on Ubuntu. reply

post.title: Ask HN: What happens when Claude Code goes away?

content.text: I have become very proficient with Claude Code and I use it for everything, both at work and in my personal life. At this point, if I lost access to it, it would be like missing a body part. At the risk of hyperbole, it makes me a better person. I am more effective in everything I do. Someday it will probably go away. I haven't had great success making Claude Code work with local Ollama/Quen.

Losing access to Claude Code - just imagine it. That's really the main reason people push for local open-source models. If you build everything around a closed cloud API, you're basicly staking your whole career on someone else's rules. Anthropic can change prices or shut down your account anytime, and suddenly, your productivity takes a nosedive. There's only one way out: leran to run your own setup. Right now, getting Claude Code to work well alongside Ollama or Qwen is tough. Context management and system instructions are tricky. But honestly, it's our only real safety net. If you can fire up quantized Qwen 2.5 coder model on your own machine, you control your workflow. Sure, it might not be as fast as Sonnet, but there's no kill-switch, no subscriptions, and no strings attached. Think of AI tools like servers: if you can't self-host a backup, you don't really own your workflow. I worked with a friend on a local AI-Agent that can code, that can talk with you about anything and can control your whole computer, even spotify it can easily search on spotify or you can say "open zapzap" or "open whatsapp" it looks for apps on your computer if nothing found with the name it opens the browser and google if you say "open youtube" it opens the browser with https://www.youtube.com . of course you can say it with your voice what you want, so you haven't write it to it per keyboard if your busy. if you wanna try just write a response here and I talk to my friend if I can make it open source. Sorry for self-promoten here but it's something about the topic. if you have a problem with the self-promoten just write a reply and I'll remove this comment. reply

I've had a Claude max plan that I've been using daily for about 6 months now.  This month I decided to turn off auto-renew and moved over to Codex to try it out.  There's virtually no switching costs.  Of course there are some slight differences I'm noticing between the two but nothing that would keep me loyal to one over the other. Also, Claude Code is the agentic harness with the underlying models being the anthropic ones.  If it's the harness you're worried about, try out Codex or any of the open source ones like OpenCode, Pi, Goose. This will never go away.  Instead it will become more local.  In the future, it's more likely that you have a model running on your computer.  These companies have no moat.  You don't need to worry about it going away or them charging beyond what you can pay. reply

Hopefully by then local models will be more useful or more accessible on decent hardware. For now, all my Codex projects include instructions to comment all code for human readers, develop unit tests, and document everything in human readable formats with a human audience in mind. Caveat: I was a pretty decent programmer before AI. reply

I irregularly use a framework similar to the one by Klein, Sonkin, Paul Johnson https://leonlins.com/writing/premortem to get one AI agent to consider the problems and potential solutions to vendor lock in. If this is for Claude specifically, feels like most common alternatives (Codex) are viable. If this is for AI agents generally, I've been backing up local model workflows as well reply

Yeah, I know how you feel.  When my tokens run out doing work, I bounce to YouTube until I'm recharged.  Claude, like prostitution, drugs, and gambling, will never go away.  That's not how markets work. reply

If Ed Zitron is to be believed, Anthropic, and all the other LLM based tools companies are bleeding cash at one of the highest burn rates in history, subsidizing your tools, and likely giving them to you at around 5-10% of their costs. Even if you're prepared to pay 10x or more for the same thing, most aren't, and they don't have a sustainable future. Your best bet is to develop a local capability on your own hardware while you've still got Claude to compare it to. Second best is to have an LLM model and harness you can run in the cloud independent of Anthropic or any other AI company. reply

post.title: Ask HN: What is the most career altering course or book you have gone through?

content.text: Pls provide link if the course materials are available anywhere.

Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware And Software by Charles Petzold. I read it in my second year of studying computer-science during the summer break, and it completely changed how I view computing. First of all, the contents alone are quite valuable, even though it is an old book, as it basically walks you through building a simple relay computer on paper, with a CPU, RAM, simplified input devices, teaches you Intel 8080 assembly as an example of assembly programming, and then even goes over a simplified BIOS, OS, GPU and higher-level languages at the end, and it does not assume you have any previous knowledge; it starts from the basic physics behind electricity, then goes into boolean algebra, logic gates, etc. It's basically computer-architecture for the layman. Beyond the content of the book, I think the biggest mark it left on me is that it taught me that there is no magic behind the layers of abstraction, and that breaking problems and concepts down into simpler ones can make what initially seems like a very complex topic into something that someone can easily follow and understand. After I read the book, a lot of things I had already learnt at university felt like they made more sense, and I then took courses like Computer Architecture and Digital Circuit Design, where I felt a lot more confident than I probably would have, had I not read that book. It definitely colored how I viewed a lot of the courses I took at university after having read it. In my career as a software developer, I still often think about that book, and I love to learn things by re-inventing the wheel and building simpler versions of complex existing software. reply

Not a book or course per say, but based on a book: The Gervais Principle, Or The Office According to "The Office" by Venkat [0] Other contenders: Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari [1] Haseeb qureshi's articles on Negotiating [2] These along with er... mind-altering substances, helped me see that reality as we live it (careers, status, institutions, ect) is like software: built/programmed by humans and can be changed by shifting your perspective.
